kind: destination_tours
status: approved
buttonLabel: "Explore tours visiting Coquesa"
lead: >-
  Coquesa is a small settlement on the northern edge of the Uyuni Salt Flat, near Tunupa Volcano. Visitors come for views across the white salt plain, a glimpse of life in high-altitude communities, and historic burial sites around the volcano. Ada Tours offers a short itinerary through Bolivia that visits the Coquesa mummies, as well as longer journeys through Peru, Bolivia, and Chile. Compare the role Coquesa plays in each itinerary and how much time to allow for this part of Uyuni.
---

## Which tours travel through Coquesa?

Our selection includes {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} with [Coquesa](/bolivia/place/coquesa/) on the main itinerary. The village sits beside the [Uyuni Salt Flat](/bolivia/place/uyuni/) near [Tunupa Volcano](/bolivia/place/tunupa-volcano/). The drive here is usually part of a longer day on the salt flat: travelers visit islands, villages, and viewpoints before returning to their overnight accommodation or continuing deeper into the Altiplano.

Ada Tours has three substantially different options. One focuses on Bolivia, combining La Paz, Lake Titicaca, and Uyuni within a week. The others cross several South American countries, with Coquesa as one stop on the Bolivian portion rather than a multi-day destination in its own right. **Choose based on the entire itinerary, not just the appearance of Coquesa on the list of places.**

## Coquesa on a seven-day journey through Bolivia

On the [“Uyuni Salt Flat, Moon Valley, La Paz and Tiwanaku” tour](/bolivia/tour/bolivia-uyuni-moon-valley-la-paz-tiwanaku/), the visit to Coquesa falls on **day 5**. After flying from La Paz, travelers set out by off-road vehicle across the [Uyuni Salt Flat](/bolivia/place/uyuni/). The route begins at the [Train Cemetery](/bolivia/place/uyuni-train-cemetery/) and [Colchani](/bolivia/place/colchani/), where visitors learn about salt processing. Stops on the salt surface and at [Incahuasi Island](/bolivia/place/incahuasi-island/), with its large cacti, follow.

After lunch, the group visits Coquesa. On this tour, you will see the historic mummies preserved around the settlement and ascend to a viewpoint on [Tunupa](/bolivia/place/tunupa-volcano/). The itinerary then returns to Uyuni. A Toyota Land Cruiser 4×4 is planned for the day; the vehicle's maximum capacity stated in the program is four passengers, a driver, and a guide.

This option suits travelers who want to experience **Coquesa as an archaeological and natural stop** without embarking on a much longer multi-country journey. The remaining days contrast the salt flat with [La Paz](/bolivia/place/la-paz/), the archaeology of Tiwanaku, and the islands of Lake Titicaca. The whole trip lasts seven days, making for a full schedule with internal drives and flights.

## Coquesa on the extended Peru, Bolivia, and Chile tour

On the [14-day Peru, Bolivia, and Chile tour](/multi-country/tour/south-america-peru-bolivia-chile-easter-island/), the Coquesa area is visited on **day 9**, during the “La Paz – Uyuni” section. After a flight, travelers continue by jeep across the salt flat, stopping at [Incahuasi](/bolivia/place/incahuasi-island/), learning about salt production in [Colchani](/bolivia/place/colchani/), and heading toward [Tahua](/bolivia/place/tahua/).

The tour description also specifically mentions a cave at the foot of the volcano containing the Coquesa mummies. Here the visit is part of a much bigger journey: exploration in Peru precedes Bolivia, and the trip then continues toward the high-altitude lagoons and Chile.

**The strength of this option is the combination of Peruvian archaeology, the salt flat, and the southern Altiplano in one journey.** That also means less time for independent walks at individual stops. If your primary aim is to explore Tunupa at length or stay in Coquesa, look closely at the day-by-day schedule rather than assuming there will be spare time.

## Coquesa on the 33-day South America itinerary

On the [33-day VIP tour of South America](/multi-country/tour/south-america-luxury-33-days/), Coquesa is scheduled for **day 16**, together with Uyuni, the [Train Cemetery](/bolivia/place/uyuni-train-cemetery/), [Colchani](/bolivia/place/colchani/), [Incahuasi](/bolivia/place/incahuasi-island/), and [Tahua](/bolivia/place/tahua/). That day includes a flight to Uyuni, an excursion across the salt flat, and accommodation at Palacio de Sal.

Unlike the preceding two itineraries, the description of this day **does not set out a separate excursion to the Coquesa mummies with its own duration or inclusions**. The village is on the itinerary, but there is no basis for assuming the visit has the same scope as on the seven-day tour.

This extended option is primarily for travelers seeking a major South American expedition with numerous stops in Peru, Bolivia, and Chile. The word VIP in the title alone does not confirm a particular vehicle type, the level of escort services, or accommodation standards at every stop: consult the details of the chosen product.

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_source_krasivaya_boliviya,tour_source_velikij_tur_po_yuzhnoj_amerike,tour_south_america_luxury_33_days}}

## What to compare before choosing an itinerary

| Option | Key difference |
|---|---|
| Bolivia, 7 days | Coquesa and the mummies on day 5 |
| South America, 14 days | Coquesa on day 9, three countries |
| South America, 33 days | Coquesa on day 16, extended itinerary |

If your goal is **to see the historic burial sites and reach a Tunupa viewpoint**, the seven-day tour describes these visits most explicitly. The 14-day option also mentions the mummy cave. The 33-day itinerary confirms a stop in the Coquesa area, but the details of what can be visited must be evaluated separately against its published terms.

The total cost and demands of a trip depend on the entire itinerary: domestic flights, number of overnight stays, length of road journeys, included excursions, and group format. Exact details for each option appear on its tour page. Do not assume one itinerary includes another's services simply because both visit Uyuni.

## Why Coquesa and Tunupa Volcano are worth visiting

[Coquesa](/bolivia/place/coquesa/) differs from the popular stops in the central [Uyuni Salt Flat](/bolivia/place/uyuni/). Here the salt flat meets inhabited settlements and volcanic slopes. On the approach, the white plain gives way to rockier, higher ground, and local roads lead toward the foot of Tunupa.

Ancient burial sites with preserved mummies are known around the settlement. A guide's explanation helps visitors understand their archaeological and cultural significance. Access to historic sites and sections of the mountain slopes may depend on local regulations and the weather. The caves and burial grounds should not be treated as unrestricted places to explore on your own.

For panoramic views of the salt flat, [Tunupa Volcano](/bolivia/place/tunupa-volcano/) offers a different perspective from [Incahuasi](/bolivia/place/incahuasi-island/): from the mainland edge, you can see the rising slopes, settlements, and the vast salt plain. Choose a viewpoint route according to the specific itinerary, since a brief stop and a separate mountain hike require very different amounts of time.

## Planning a visit to Coquesa

Much of the journey takes place at high altitude. [Uyuni](/bolivia/place/uyuni/) itself lies at approximately 3,600 m, and the altitude increases toward the volcanic viewpoints. If you are arriving on the Altiplano for the first time, allow for acclimatization, the exertion of walking, and cold mornings and evenings.

In the dry months, the white salt crust and roads along the edge look very different from those of the rainy season. When water covers parts of Uyuni, the famous sky reflections appear, but some sections may become impassable. Weather can change the order of stops and access to viewpoints. Neither the iconic mirror effect nor access to every location can be guaranteed in advance.

Bring warm clothes, sun protection, water, and shoes with reliable grip. Shade is scarce on the salt flat and exposed slopes; sunlight can be intense during the day, while temperatures fall markedly after sunset. When choosing a trip that includes historical sites, confirm what the visit covers rather than relying solely on Coquesa's name in the list of stops.

## Frequently asked questions

### Which Ada Tours itineraries include Coquesa?

Our selection includes routes with Coquesa on the main itinerary. Options range from seven days in Bolivia to 14- and 33-day journeys through several countries. Check the stops in the selection on this page and in the individual tour descriptions.

### Do all tours include an excursion to the Coquesa mummies?

There is no basis for saying that all do. The historic burial sites are explicitly mentioned in the seven- and 14-day tours. The 33-day itinerary lists Coquesa among the visited places but does not describe a separate mummy visit that day.

### Can Coquesa and Uyuni be visited in a single day?

Yes. Existing Ada Tours itineraries combine Coquesa with other stops on the salt flat in one day. This normally involves a long journey by road, and the sights visited depend on the tour chosen.

### Is it necessary to climb to the summit of Tunupa?

No. The seven-day itinerary includes a viewpoint, not a full ascent to the summit. You cannot infer independent trekking arrangements or specialist guiding services from that description.

### Which option should I choose if Coquesa is my main goal?

Start with the [seven-day Bolivia itinerary](/bolivia/tour/bolivia-uyuni-moon-valley-la-paz-tiwanaku/): it gives the clearest account of visiting Coquesa, the historic mummies, and the Tunupa viewpoint. Longer journeys make more sense if you also want to explore other countries or a much wider variety of natural attractions.

lead: >-
  Coroico is a mountain town in Bolivia's Yungas region, where the cool Andean highlands give way to warm, green valleys. Visitors come to relax among forested hillsides, walk to waterfalls, learn about coffee, and travel along the famous Death Road. The routes vary in difficulty: a relaxed day in town and an active downhill cycling adventure require different preparation.
---

## Coroico: a mountain retreat in Bolivia's Yungas region

Coroico lies in the La Paz department of [Bolivia](/bolivia/), in the Yungas region. Here the Andes gradually descend toward warmer, wetter valleys connected to the Amazon Basin. This transitional geography explains the variety of landscapes: wooded slopes rise above the town, clouds and fog gather along the road, and tropical crops grow farther down.

Coroico is often chosen as a place to rest after high-altitude La Paz. Instead of the thin air of the Altiplano, travelers find green mountains, a milder climate, and opportunities to enjoy terraces, walks, and excursions to natural attractions.

Yet the town is more than a place to relax. Waterfalls, agricultural land, and active-tourism routes lie nearby. When choosing a suitable itinerary, distinguish between leisurely outings and activities involving greater physical exertion.

## Things to see and do in Coroico

### Town walks and views across the valleys

In central Coroico, you can stroll through the square, small streets, and viewpoints. The town is built on a hillside, so walks frequently open up views of the green valleys. Cafés and restaurants provide somewhere to pause after the drive through the mountains.

Early mornings often look different from midday as mist and clouds gradually reveal the scenery. Clear views, however, are not guaranteed even during the less rainy season.

### Waterfalls and forest trails

Excursions to waterfalls and short walks through forested areas can be arranged around Coroico. Our itinerary may include several waterfalls, although their specific names and the order of stops depend on the trip selected.

River outings require attention to water levels. During heavy rain, some paths become slippery and descents to the water dangerous. Even an apparently easy walk calls for suitable footwear and an assessment of the weather.

### Coffee and fruit plantations

The Yungas region is known for crops grown in its warmer valleys, including coffee, citrus fruit, and other plants. A plantation visit provides insight into cultivation and the local economy. However, touring a coffee farm, attending a tasting, and taking a specialist-led production tour are distinct experiences. Each must be confirmed separately.

Coffee and citrus plantations are found in the countryside around Coroico. They offer an opportunity to complement a nature-focused visit with an introduction to rural life. You can compare similar journeys in our [food and wine section](/interests/food-and-wine/) without assuming that every trip to Yungas is a dedicated coffee tour.

## How Death Road and Coroico are connected

One of the best-known routes in the region is the old road through the northern Yungas, commonly called **Death Road** (Camino de la Muerte). Its narrow stretches, sheer drop-offs, and frequent cloud cover long made it a difficult route between the highlands and the valleys.

Today the historic road is also known for organized downhill bicycle rides. The route traverses dramatic changes in altitude, vegetation, and temperature. This is a separate adventure requiring specialist equipment and safety procedures, not an ordinary sightseeing excursion around Coroico.

If your trip focuses solely on relaxing in town, downhill cycling may not feature in the program at all. If it is included, check the route, participant requirements, protective gear, support vehicle, and which road sections will actually be used. The Death Road experience involves genuine risks and requires a qualified operator.

## Best time to visit Coroico

The Yungas climate is considerably warmer and wetter than the high-altitude plateau. During the drier part of the year, walks and road journeys are generally easier to plan. In the rainy months, vegetation becomes especially lush, but clouds, heavy rainfall, and muddy trails are more common.

Plan around your main goal. If mountain views and road trips are important, check the weather and road conditions. Short walks around town may still be comfortable in the rainy season. Waterfalls and downhill cycling require more careful safety planning.

You will also need clothing for different elevations: a journey from La Paz to Coroico passes through areas with very different temperatures. The first section may be cool and windy, while in the Yungas light clothing, rain protection, and insect repellent will come in handy.

## Getting there and adding Coroico to a Bolivia itinerary

Coroico is connected to La Paz by road. The drive is an experience in itself as high-altitude landscapes gradually change into wooded valleys. When planning, confirm the road to be used and the journey time under current conditions: the historic Death Road and modern transport connections are not the same thing.

You can stay in town to rest and enjoy unhurried walks, then head to waterfalls or agricultural sites the next day. This pacing makes particular sense after a demanding high-altitude itinerary. However, the number of nights, included transfers, excursions, and meals always depends on the specific package selected.

Our [Bolivia tour catalog](/bolivia/tour/) lets you compare routes by their actual geography. Travelers interested in more active trips can also explore the [adventure section](/interests/adventure/), which distinguishes a peaceful stay in Yungas from an organized downhill bike ride or canyoning.

## Frequently asked questions about Coroico

### Where is Coroico?

In Bolivia's La Paz department, in the Yungas region, where the high Andes descend toward warmer, wetter valleys.

### Are Coroico and Death Road the same place?

No. Coroico is a town and a base for exploring the region. Death Road is a historic mountain route, with downhill cycling excursions on certain sections.

### Are there coffee plantations in Coroico?

Coffee is grown in the Yungas region, and tourism descriptions of Coroico mention visits to coffee and fruit farms. Availability of a visit to a specific farm must be checked in the itinerary.

### Is Coroico suitable for a relaxing holiday?

Yes. You can limit your visit to walks around town and mountain views. Waterfalls, canyoning, and journeys along Death Road require separate planning and preparation.

lead: >-
  Cuevas Waterfalls lie in the green foothills near Samaipata in Bolivia's Santa Cruz department. This is a destination for a short nature walk beside the river and cascades, easily included in a journey through the Samaipata valleys and the surroundings of Amboró National Park.
---

## Cuevas Waterfalls in Bolivia: a riverside walk near Samaipata

[Cuevas Waterfalls](/bolivia/place/cuevas-waterfalls/) (Cascadas de Cuevas) lie in the sub-Andean valleys of the Santa Cruz department, near [Samaipata](/bolivia/place/samaipata/). This natural attraction features river cascades, green slopes, and paths along the water. For travelers, it is primarily a peaceful stop after exploring the region's historical and natural sights.

**Cuevas is very different from Bolivia's dry, high-altitude Altiplano.** Here you find more vegetation, humid air, and river scenery. After drives between towns and visits to archaeological sites, a walk along a shaded path reveals a different natural environment within the country.

## Where are Cuevas Waterfalls?

The Samaipata area lies west of the city of Santa Cruz de la Sierra, on the transition toward the Andean foothills. Travelers set out from here to the El Fuerte archaeological complex, the natural areas of Amboró, and river waterfalls. Cuevas sits amid green hills near the road connecting this tourist area to the Santa Cruz lowlands.

The waterfalls are most conveniently visited as part of a journey around Samaipata. When planning, check the condition of the local access road, walking time, and entry arrangements for the natural area. The condition of paths and permitted rest areas may change during the rainy season.

## What to see around the cascades

### Walking along the river

The main route follows a trail along the watercourse and a series of small waterfalls. Local visitor descriptions of Cascadas de Cuevas mention several cascades, vegetated stretches, and natural pools. In places you can stop by the water and watch it flow between the rocks.

The area is best enjoyed at an unhurried pace. There is no need to rush to every cascade: wet rocks and unpaved sections require care. When it rains, the riverside trail can become slippery.

### Water and natural pools

Pools and natural basins occur near the waterfalls. Their appearance depends on rainfall, the season, and river levels. Before swimming, check local rules and the current. Photographs of calm water are no guarantee of safe swimming at another time.

Comfortable shoes, drinking water, and protection from sun or rain are useful for the walk. A change of clothes is handy if you plan to spend time by the water in permitted areas. Take your rubbish away and avoid damaging vegetation or the riverbanks.

### Vegetation in the sub-Andean valleys

Cuevas is interesting for more than the water alone. Shades of green vary across the landscape, with shrubs, trees, and plants growing in damp areas. After the desert scenery so often associated with Bolivia, this region reveals a gentler and wetter side of the country.

Wildlife watching should not be treated as an essential objective of a short stop. If biodiversity is your main interest, arrange a dedicated guided route through the region's natural areas.

## Cuevas, Samaipata, and Amboró: planning your day

These three names often appear on one itinerary, but they represent different experiences.

| Place | Main reason to visit |
|---|---|
| [Cuevas](/bolivia/place/cuevas-waterfalls/) | Waterfalls and a riverside walk |
| [Samaipata](/bolivia/place/samaipata/) | The town and its archaeological heritage |
| Amboró National Park | Forests, plants, and nature watching |

[Samaipata](/bolivia/place/samaipata/) is known for El Fuerte, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. This archaeological monument has an extensive carved rock surface and a history linked to different cultures. Cuevas Waterfalls offer something entirely different: the river and its natural surroundings are the main attraction.

The Amboró National Park area offers forest trails. The duration and guiding arrangements for hikes can be quite different from a brief stop at the waterfalls. Do not assume that all three places are automatically included in a single excursion.

If you plan to see both El Fuerte and the forest, decide in advance how much time remains for Cuevas. On a busy itinerary, the cascades may be a short stop on the way; a more flexible schedule allows for a longer, independent break.

## When to visit the waterfalls

The weather on the day of your visit and rainfall in the preceding days are the most important factors. After rain, the flow may become stronger and change color, while dirt trails get more slippery. In a dry spell, the water may appear calmer. The waterfalls cannot be expected to look the same throughout the year.

Before setting out, check road access, opening hours, and whether your chosen trail is passable. For families with children or travelers with limited mobility, the actual trail surface matters: a natural riverside path may include steps, stones, and slippery sections.

## Cuevas Waterfalls on an Ada Tours itinerary

The first days of the [12-day “Treasures of Bolivia” itinerary](/bolivia/tour/bolivia-treasures-12-days/) take travelers through Santa Cruz, Samaipata, and the natural area of Amboró. On the return from the cloud forest, the itinerary includes a stop at Cuevas Waterfalls. The journey later continues to Sucre, Potosí, and [Uyuni](/bolivia/place/uyuni/).

This shows how waterfalls complement an extended journey combining humid foothills and dry high-altitude landscapes. The time spent by the water, separate entry fees, and any additional services should be checked against this particular tour program. A stop does not imply that swimming or a dedicated excursion to each cascade is included.

## Frequently asked questions about Cuevas Waterfalls

### How far is Cuevas from Samaipata?

The waterfalls are in the Samaipata area, making them a convenient addition to a visit to the surroundings. The exact journey time depends on the starting point, road conditions, and means of transport.

### Can visitors swim in the natural pools?

That depends on local permission and current river conditions. After rain, the current and slippery approaches may make swimming inadvisable or prohibited.

### Are Cuevas Waterfalls and Amboró National Park the same place?

No. Cuevas is a group of river waterfalls; Amboró is a much larger protected natural area with separate trails. You can combine them in a trip, but they require different planning.

### Are the waterfalls suitable for a short stop?

Yes, provided the trail is accessible and the visit is arranged in advance. For this type of visit, it is particularly important not to plan several distant excursions on the same day.

## Which Ada Tours itinerary visits Cuevas Waterfalls?

We offer {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} that include [Cuevas Waterfalls](/bolivia/place/cuevas-waterfalls/) on the main route. The confirmed program is [“Treasures of Bolivia,” a 12-day journey](/bolivia/tour/bolivia-treasures-12-days/). It begins around [Santa Cruz](/bolivia/place/santa-cruz/), passes through [Samaipata](/bolivia/place/samaipata/) and [Amboró National Park](/bolivia/place/amboro-national-park/), then continues through the country's historic cities and high-altitude regions.

For travelers, this is an appealing combination of two natural experiences in one day: a morning walk through Amboró's humid forest and a stop at the waterfalls on the return drive. It is important, however, to distinguish **Cuevas appearing on the itinerary** from a separate excursion with a fixed swimming period, equipment, or extended trekking. Those services are not listed in the day's description.

## Day 3: Amboró, Cuevas, and the return to Santa Cruz

On **day 3**, after breakfast, the tour heads to [Amboró National Park](/bolivia/place/amboro-national-park/) and its cloud-forest area. During the visit, you walk among characteristic local vegetation, including large ferns. This is a different environment from the dry highlands for which western Bolivia is famous: humid slopes, dense greenery, and woodland trails.

**In the afternoon, the group returns toward Santa Cruz, stopping at Cuevas Waterfalls along the way.** The falls are surrounded by thick vegetation, and the water in the cascades is clear. Following the nature-focused part of the journey, the group returns to the city for a night at LP Equipetrol.

On this itinerary, Cuevas is **part of a day with two nature stops**, rather than a separate multi-day hike. It is a good introduction to Bolivia's green foothills for travelers wishing to combine forests and waterfalls before continuing through the country.

## What happens before and after the waterfalls?

The itinerary follows a set sequence, with no separate return to Cuevas later in the trip.

| Day | Main activities |
|---|---|
| 2 | [Samaipata](/bolivia/place/samaipata/) |
| 3 | [Amboró](/bolivia/place/amboro-national-park/) and Cuevas |
| 4 | Flight to [Sucre](/bolivia/place/sucre/) |

On **day 2**, guests travel from the Santa Cruz area to Samaipata. It is known for the El Fuerte archaeological complex and its proximity to natural areas of the eastern Andean foothills. This provides a cultural perspective ahead of the following day's forest visit.

On **day 4**, the journey continues with a flight from Santa Cruz to [Sucre](/bolivia/place/sucre/). The route then takes in historic cities, including [Potosí](/bolivia/place/potosi/), the [Uyuni Salt Flat](/bolivia/place/uyuni/), and the southwestern highlands. Confirmed stops on the itinerary include [Laguna Colorada](/bolivia/place/laguna-colorada/) and the [Eduardo Avaroa Reserve](/bolivia/place/eduardo-avaroa-national-reserve/).

This sequence explains the main advantage of the 12-day tour: one journey combines the wooded Samaipata area, historic urban centers, and the very different nature of the Altiplano. If spending an entire day at Cuevas is your main goal, this stop should not be treated as the equivalent of a separate waterfalls itinerary.

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_source_sokrovishcha_bolivii}}

## How Cuevas Waterfalls differ from Amboró National Park

[Cuevas](/bolivia/place/cuevas-waterfalls/) is a specific natural attraction with cascades, a stream, and small pools. It is approximately 20 km from [Samaipata](/bolivia/place/samaipata/), along the road toward Santa Cruz. Three waterfalls are known in this area, connected by walking sections. But our tour includes **a stop at the waterfalls**, without promising a separate visit to all three.

[Amboró National Park](/bolivia/place/amboro-national-park/) is an extensive protected area with forests and complex terrain. The current tour visits it for a cloud-forest walk, rather than to view a waterfall as the sole focus of the day. Cuevas lies in the same tourist region, but proximity to the park does not mean that access rules, entrance tickets, or walking arrangements are identical.

The choice is straightforward: for humid forest and ferns, the morning part of the [Amboró excursion](/bolivia/place/amboro-national-park/) is more relevant; for cascades and time beside the water, the stop at Cuevas is the highlight. Combining the two offers different natural settings within a single itinerary day.

## When to visit the waterfalls

Bolivia's eastern foothills are much wetter than the Uyuni Salt Flat and most of the Altiplano. During the rainy months, the cascades usually carry more water, but stones and dirt paths can become slippery. Heavy rainfall can sometimes restrict access to certain areas because of water levels and trail conditions.

Drier weather may make walking more comfortable, although the volume of water and appearance of the cascades will be different. There is no guaranteed waterfall condition for a particular date: recent rainfall, local weather, and stream levels all matter.

If your main aim is to combine Cuevas with high-altitude [Uyuni](/bolivia/place/uyuni/), select the season for the entire itinerary. Weather at the waterfalls differs from conditions on the salt flat: a season well suited to the green eastern valleys may not offer dry salt crusts or mirror-like reflections at Uyuni.

## Preparing for the stop at Cuevas

For a short walk, wear shoes with reliable grip on wet ground. Light rain protection, drinking water, and clothing appropriate for a warm, humid day are useful. Stones near the cascades may be slippery even in good weather.

Natural pools in the Cuevas area are sometimes used for swimming. But **swimming is not listed as a separately included activity on the 12-day Ada Tours itinerary**. Whether it is possible depends on local conditions, the time available at the stop, and local rules. Do not schedule swimming as an obligatory activity or assume towels, changing facilities, or special supervision are provided: none of those services are specified in the chosen program.

Unlike visits to the high-altitude lagoons, reaching Cuevas does not involve crossing several remote desert regions. It lies conveniently on the route from [Samaipata](/bolivia/place/samaipata/) to [Santa Cruz](/bolivia/place/santa-cruz/), as used by the current tour. An independent visit would require organizing return transport separately. On the Ada Tours itinerary, transport is included as part of the overall transfer, but no standalone excursion with an open schedule is offered here.

## Who will enjoy this itinerary?

**Choose the 12-day “Treasures of Bolivia” tour** if you want to explore very different parts of the country: green valleys, historic cities, the salt flat, and lagoons. Cuevas Waterfalls add a natural stop that is easily missed on a trip focusing only on La Paz and Uyuni.

If tropical vegetation is your main interest, compare the [tour through Amboró National Park](/bolivia/place/amboro-national-park/tour/) and other options in the [Bolivia travel catalog](/bolivia/tour/). This helps distinguish tours with a forest walk from those with viewpoints only or a main emphasis on historical towns and the Altiplano. If Cuevas is not mentioned on another itinerary, its inclusion should not be promised by analogy.

## Frequently asked questions

### On which day of the tour are Cuevas Waterfalls visited?

On the [12-day “Treasures of Bolivia” journey](/bolivia/tour/bolivia-treasures-12-days/), Cuevas is visited on **day 3**, after Amboró National Park and before returning to Santa Cruz.

### Can Cuevas be combined with Amboró National Park?

Yes. That is precisely the combination in the current tour: a cloud-forest walk first, followed by a waterfall stop. They are two separate natural attractions, however, and their entry and visiting conditions should not be confused.

### Is swimming at the waterfalls included in the tour price?

The itinerary includes a visit to Cuevas Waterfalls but does not list swimming as a separate included activity. It therefore cannot be regarded as a guaranteed service.

### Do I need to allow a separate day for Cuevas?

Not on the confirmed Ada Tours itinerary: the stop is included in the journey between the nature excursion and Santa Cruz. If you want to walk to all the cascades and spend an extended period relaxing beside the water, that calls for different planning.

### Are Cuevas Waterfalls in the high-altitude part of Bolivia?

No. They lie in the eastern Andean foothills near Samaipata, with much wetter vegetation. The [Uyuni Salt Flat](/bolivia/place/uyuni/) and [Eduardo Avaroa Reserve](/bolivia/place/eduardo-avaroa-national-reserve/) are in an entirely different natural region, so weather and clothing requirements differ.

## Eduardo Avaroa Reserve: Bolivia's flamingos, lagoons, and volcanoes

The Eduardo Avaroa Andean Fauna National Reserve lies in the Lípez region of southwestern Bolivia, near Chile. Its landscapes include desiccated plains, mineral lagoons, volcanoes, and geothermal fields. It is one of the most fascinating natural areas for travelers planning an overland journey through the highlands.

A visit requires carefully planned transport: unpaved roads connect the stops, while high altitude, wind, and cold affect visitors' well-being and the length of journeys.

## Laguna Colorada and flamingos

[Laguna Colorada](/bolivia/place/laguna-colorada/) is known for its reddish water and flamingos in the shallows. Reports by Bolivia's SERNAP protected-areas authority note Andean flamingos, Chilean flamingos, and James's flamingos. Bird numbers change with the season, while the water's colors vary with natural conditions and light.

For that reason, it is impossible to guarantee a particular shade of red in photographs or an encounter with a specific flamingo species. Respect the protected area's restrictions and do not disturb wildlife around the lagoons.

## Sol de Mañana geysers and the Siloli Desert

[Sol de Mañana](/bolivia/place/sol-de-manana-geysers/) is an area of steam vents and hot mud pools. Follow your guide's instructions carefully: ground around thermal features may be unstable.

The [Siloli Desert](/bolivia/place/siloli-desert/) features rock formations and dry volcanic scenery. Elsewhere along the routes are [Laguna Verde](/bolivia/place/laguna-verde/), Cañapa, Hedionda, and [Honda](/bolivia/place/laguna-honda/) lagoons. However, each individual tour's route must be checked: mentioning the region does not guarantee a visit to every lagoon.

## Which Ada Tours itineraries visit the reserve?

On the [three-day off-road tour across Uyuni](/bolivia/tour/bolivia-uyuni-salt-flats-jeep-tour-3-days/), the reserve is part of a route from the Hito Cajones border crossing through Laguna Verde, Sol de Mañana, and Laguna Colorada to the salt flat. This format suits travelers who want to dedicate several days specifically to the deserts and lagoons.

When choosing, compare the starting point, number of overnight stays, and sequence of days at altitude.

## Altitude, temperatures, and safety

Many stops are above 4,000 m. Even in bright sunshine, it can be cold and very windy, with large changes in temperature between day and night. Bring warm layers, drinking water, sun protection, and plan a gentle pace. Discuss high-altitude travel with a doctor beforehand, particularly if you have a chronic medical condition.

Entrance fees, meals, accommodation, and vehicle equipment should be checked for each specific tour. They cannot be assumed to be included in every itinerary simply because it visits the same reserve.

## Frequently asked questions about the reserve

### Can you always see flamingos?

Flamingos inhabit the region, but their numbers, location, and visibility change.

### Is Eduardo Avaroa Reserve the same as the Uyuni Salt Flat?

No. The [Uyuni Salt Flat](/bolivia/place/uyuni/) is a separate salt plain. The reserve encompasses lagoons, volcanic areas, and flamingo habitats, and tours often combine the two.

### Is it safe to walk near the geysers?

Only in approved areas with a guide. Hot mud and unstable ground are dangerous.
